sources.title: Peter Jackson: Golden Horde, Encyclopaedia Iranica
sources.note: Jochid dynasty, Batu’s conquests, Berke and Öz Beg, Sarai, Mamluk alliance, civil war and Tokhtamysh.

sources.title: UC Berkeley ORIAS: Ibn Battuta in the lands of the Golden Horde
sources.note: Attributed fourteenth-century travel observations: mobile households, elite women, food and Black Sea trade. Use the 1330s broadly; the teaching page contains unrelated oversimplifications not repeated here.

sources.title: UNESCO: Bolgar Historical and Archaeological Complex
sources.note: Outstanding Universal Value: surviving urban structures, cultural exchanges and continuity through successive political regimes.

sources.title: Bolgar World Heritage nomination dossier
sources.note: Historical development section: fourteenth-century workshops, educational institutions, water supply and drainage. State Party submission, not independent confirmation of every historical claim.

sources.title: Kvitkovskyi and Svystun: Materials of the Golden Horde period from Kitsivka 1
sources.note: 2023 archaeological report, DOI 10.37445/adiu.2023.03.06: late-thirteenth and fourteenth-century settlement materials at a Siverskyi Donets crossing.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art: Helmet, object 32641
sources.note: Steel and silver helmet, probably circa 1342-1357; proposed identification of the Arabic inscription with Jani Beg is conditional.

sources.title: Ashmolean Museum: silver half-dirham HCR15711
sources.note: Tokhtamysh coin attributed to Mahmudabad, circa 1376-1395; obverse Arabic inscription, translation and physical measurements.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Persian manuscripts in Italy
sources.note: Venice section, Codex Cumanicus in the Biblioteca Marciana, with Latin, Persian and Cuman vocabulary; fourteenth-century compilation and transmission.

sources.title: Emma Zilivinskaya: The Golden Horde Baths
sources.note: 2002 archaeological paper, pp. 126-130: 25 excavated baths known to the author, 14 communal and 11 private; hammams and ritual washing.

sources.title: L. F. Abzalov: Hydropathy in the Golden Horde
sources.note: 2017 study, pp. 756-769: reports of hot and mineral springs and bathing as historical treatment; not evidence of modern clinical efficacy.

sources.title: L. F. Abzalov: Bimaristan in the Golden Horde
sources.note: 2020 article, printed pp. 457-471, English abstract p. 458: Urgench hospital in Ibn Battuta and al-Birzali; reconstruction and possible hospitals elsewhere are explicitly hypotheses.

sources.title: Istvan Vasary: The Crimean Khanate and the Great Horde, a fight for primacy
sources.note: Chapter in Denise Klein, ed., 2012, pp. 13-26: Great Horde chronology and disputed destruction of Sarai.

proposedOverrides.name: Golden Horde
proposedOverrides.summary: The Golden Horde connected the Eurasian steppe with cities and long-distance trade. Its people built bathhouses, minted inscribed coins and compiled multilingual books. This map interval shows part of its history, which later continued through competing successor khanates.

identityEvidence.assessment: Broad imported Golden Horde label confirmed. Coverage interval retained, not treated as foundation or extinction; exact territorial extent remains unverified.

proposedOverrides.name: Great Horde
proposedOverrides.summary: The Great Horde claimed the Golden Horde’s inheritance. Defeat in 1502 changed political power; its people survived.

identityEvidence.assessment: Late imported Golden Horde label and lower-Volga location support Great Horde identification; imported 1530 endpoint replaced by historical 1502 defeat. Exact territorial extent remains unverified.
